title: Protest of Anna Farrar re Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc’s filing to establish the Large Load Addition Resource Study under ER27-25.

documents.name: FERC_Protest_Anna_Farrar.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.      Docket No. ER27-25-000


                             PROTEST OF ANNA FARRAR


 Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's Rules of Practice

 and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.211, I, Anna Farrar, submit this protest of specified

 provisions of the Large Load Addition Resource Study (LARS) tariff revisions filed by

 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO) on October 2, 2026, Docket

 No. ER27-25-000 (Accession No. 20261002-5074). [1] This protest concerns the

 proposed federal tariff process, not authorization of any particular Missouri development.

 I reside in Warren County, Missouri, and receive residential electric service from

 Ameren Missouri (Union Electric Company). I support reliable and efficient review of

 large loads and associated generation. My objection is to accepting a new accelerated

 process without sufficient explanation of the financial consequences of transmission

 constraints attributable to overlapping study assumptions and the treatment of upgrades

 identified later.


 I. THE PROPOSAL INCLUDES MEANINGFUL SAFEGUARDS

 The October 2 proposed clean tariff, Attachment X § 3.12.4, distinguishes mitigation

 identified only through generation-interconnection studies from mitigation identified

 through transmission or common study results. The former is assigned as a Generator

 Interconnection Project (GIP); the latter is classified as a Baseline Reliability Project

 (BRP) or Other project under applicable tariff rules. Attachment X § 3.12.7.4 addresses

 specified continuing obligations for assigned upgrades if the generator or associated large

 load withdraws. [1]


Docket No. ER27-25-000                                                                       1
  MISO also proposes load-study scenarios incorporating other planned load additions, and

 evaluates the loss of associated generation. [1] I do not allege that the proposal lacks

 cumulative modeling, outage analysis, or all financial protections. The narrower question

 is whether these provisions adequately address additional transmission upgrades that are

 first identified through a subsequent planning cycle because two separate studies relied

 on overlapping available capacity.


 II. MISO IDENTIFIES A DISTINCT RISK FROM OVERLAPPING STUDIES

 MISO's transmittal letter discusses a potential overallocation of available transmission

 capacity between the LARS process and the existing Definitive Planning Phase (DPP)

 generator-interconnection process. It contemplates addressing resulting constraints

 through a subsequent MISO Transmission Expansion Plan (MTEP) project, with the cost

 assigned under existing tariff mechanisms, likely to load in the affected Transmission

 Pricing Zone. Drake characterizes the risk of overallocation as minimal. Transmittal

 Letter at 13; Drake Testimony at 33. [1]

 In the supporting prepared testimony, Christina Drake explains that the overlapping

 LARS and DPP projects could proceed without additional charges arising from that

 overallocation, while the constraint is addressed through later transmission planning.

 Drake Testimony at 33 (combined filing PDF at 1511). [1]

 This is a concrete concern about cost causation and the reasonableness of the proposed

 procedure. I do not claim any current unlawful charge, nor do I assume that all future

 MTEP expenditures must be borne exclusively by an individual large load. A later

 upgrade may provide identifiable benefits to the wider network. But MISO should

 explain why the costs associated with reconciling overlapping study assumptions would

 appropriately fall on the affected pricing zone instead of being attributed, in whole or in

 part, to the projects whose concurrent studies created the conflict.




Docket No. ER27-25-000                                                                         2
  FERC has separately identified the lack of public transparency regarding large-load

 network upgrades and the risk that costs of unbuilt or undersubscribed large loads may

 shift to other transmission customers. The Commission's findings in its June 18, 2026

 Section 206 show-cause order are preliminary; this protest does not present them as a

 final adjudication of any LARS cost allocation. EL26-70-000, 195 FERC ¶ 61,212, at

 paragraphs 71-83. [2]


 III. PROJECT CLASSIFICATION IS NOT THE SAME AS VERIFIED COST
 CAUSATION

 Where the same constraint appears in both studies, the proposed tariff's BRP or Other

 classification may be justified by shared reliability benefits. It does not, by itself, answer

 which portion of an upgrade is attributable to the new load, the associated generation, or

 an independently existing reliability need. Attachment X § 3.12.4. [1]

 The Commission should require MISO to identify what records and comparison studies

 will be available to substantiate causation: the relevant with-load and without-load

 assumptions, the effects of associated generation, the scope and estimated costs of

 incremental upgrades, the affected pricing zones, the governing allocation rules, and any

 contributions or credits that prevent double recovery. Such information would allow

 regulators and transmission customers to examine both legitimate shared benefits and

 potential unjustified cost shifting.




Docket No. ER27-25-000                                                                            3
  IV. MISSOURI RECORDS SHOW MULTIPLE LARGE-LOAD STUDIES AND
 NETWORK CHANGES

 MISO's April 7, 2025 Expedited Project Review (EPR) for Project P50616 documents a

 proposed 200-MW data-center load at Ameren's Rootbeer 345-kV substation, possible

 future expansion, and an estimated $5 million project cost. MISO reported no new

 reliability violations in the studied scenarios. [3] MISO's February 5, 2024 EPR for

 P50086 documents a separate proposed 250-MW data-center load at Montgomery's

 161-kV facilities and names Navier, Inc. as the customer. That study likewise reported no

 new violations in its reviewed scenarios. [4] These are proposed loads reviewed under

 EPR, not demonstrated applications under LARS.

 The facilities are electrically connected, rather than simply nearby on a map. Ameren

 witness Justin D. Wenk identifies the existing Montgomery-Rootbeer 345-kV line and

 describes relocating its terminal as part of the proposed Montgomery-Callaway

 Connector work in Missouri PSC File No. EA-2026-0058. Wenk Direct Testimony at 4.

 [5] Ameren witness Steven M. Wills separately explains that Rootbeer was originally

 developed for the Split Rail solar interconnection, before the large-load proposals, and

 states Ameren's expectation that large-load retail revenues would contribute toward

 shared network transmission expenses. The Split Rail interconnection agreement

 allocated the cost of a reserved future Rootbeer terminal to the entity creating the need

 for it. Wills Surrebuttal at 15-16; Schedule SMW-S1, original Sheet 88. [6] The

 Montgomery-Callaway Connector's stated generation-related purpose should not be

 conflated with proven data-center cost causation.

 The scale of the evolving network is also documented by MISO. Its November 4, 2025

 EPR results identify a 1,000-MW load at the planned Elkhorn substation (P50737) and a

 400-MW load at Yoshi (P50738), with proposed 345-kV connections involving

 Lumberjack, the Odyssey-Montgomery corridor, and Scarlet. MISO's Elkhorn study



Docket No. ER27-25-000                                                                       4
  identified two corrective-action projects, including P51113, a $5 million Baseline

 Reliability Project proposal to upgrade Montgomery 345-kV terminal equipment to 4,000

 amperes following identified thermal observations. MISO recommended advancement

 into MTEP26 Appendix A. This is evidence of studied mitigation needs, not proof that

 these facilities are built or that the proposed projects have been granted final approval.

 [8]

 Ameren Missouri's October 19, 2026 Crossroads Connector announcement identifies a

 further approximately 22 miles of proposed double-circuit 345-kV transmission in

 Warren and Montgomery counties. Phase 1 would link Lumberjack to the

 Montgomery-Callaway corridor; Phase 2 would link a new Float substation west of

 Warrenton with the Nightingale and Lumberjack substations. Ameren expressly

 describes the project as intended to meet anticipated nearby data-center demand. Ameren

 says those customers pay direct interconnection costs up front and that it will seek future

 Missouri PSC approval for rates covering the remaining Crossroads costs. Those are

 Ameren's representations and proposed future rate treatment, not a final determination

 that all project costs have been recovered or assigned. [9]

 Together, these official records establish an expanding set of major load additions,

 planned transmission paths, and at least one specifically identified load-study corrective

 action. Their relevance here is methodological: MISO should explain how LARS

 preserves consistent cumulative assumptions across EPR, DPP, and MTEP, distinguishes

 existing or generation-driven facilities from incremental large-load-driven costs, and

 retains the evidence needed to attribute later upgrades appropriately. I do not claim that

 the named Missouri projects are LARS applicants, that all planned lines form a

 completed operational loop, or that every shared transmission improvement was caused

 by data centers.




Docket No. ER27-25-000                                                                         5
  V. THE SEPARATE COST-RECOVERY FRAMEWORK SHOULD NOT LEAVE
 A GAP

 MISO's transmittal letter anticipates a further Section 205 filing concerning pro forma

 large-load cost-recovery protections by November 16, 2026. MISO states that LARS can

 be implemented under the present proposal without awaiting those later tariff protections.

 The proposal also addresses the availability of later Affected System study results.

 Transmittal Letter at 14 n.66; Attachment X § 3.12.4. [1] An anticipated future filing

 cannot itself establish enforceable obligations in this docket.

 MISO should explain whether the proposed withdrawal and assigned-project obligations

 extend to constraints and upgrades caused by study overallocation but identified only

 through a later MTEP cycle; which transmission customer or generator bears such

 obligations; when financial security becomes binding; and how state retail charges and

 federal transmission recovery will be reconciled to avoid duplicate collections and

 financial gaps.

 Missouri PSC File No. ET-2025-0184 contains an approved Ameren Missouri large-load

 rate plan. [7] That retail tariff does not by its existence prove that every shared, federally

 jurisdictional MISO transmission obligation is secured from the ultimate large-load

 customer. This concern parallels FERC's preliminary findings on transparency and

 large-load cost-recovery agreements in EL26-70-000. [2]




Docket No. ER27-25-000                                                                            6
  VI. REQUESTED COMMISSION ACTION

 I respectfully request that the Commission: (1) require MISO to substantiate its

 assessment that the risk of LARS/DPP transmission-capacity overallocation is minimal

 and explain who would bear resulting MTEP costs; (2) require an explanation of how

 LARS models previously reviewed EPR loads and planned network changes affecting

 shared facilities, and a transparent basis for identifying and allocating later-discovered

 upgrades, including projects classified as BRP or Other; (3) explain the binding effect

 and timing of any cost-recovery security, the treatment of later Affected System

 obligations, and credits needed to avoid double recovery; and (4) require an adequate

 explanation or appropriate tariff changes before accepting the proposal without

 conditions, or take such other action as permitted under Section 205 of the Federal Power

 Act.

 This protest does not ask FERC to reassign the entire cost of any named Missouri

 transmission facility to a data-center developer or to determine Missouri retail rates. It

 asks for an adequately supported, reviewable federal study and cost-responsibility

 process.


 Respectfully submitted,

 /s/ Anna Farrar

 Anna Farrar

 Individual Protestant, appearing pro se

 P.O. Box 161

 Warrenton, MO 63383

 Email for service: anna.farrar@wccrd.com

 Telephone: 636-235-6889

Docket No. ER27-25-000                                                                        7

 [5] Missouri PSC, File EA-2026-0058, Justin D. Wenk, Direct Testimony (Nov. 10, 2025), printed pp.

 [6] Missouri PSC, File EA-2025-0238, Steven M. Wills, Surrebuttal Testimony (Jan. 16, 2026),

 printed pp. 15-16, and Schedule SMW-S1, original Sheet 88. Official PSC testimony and agreement

 [7] Missouri PSC, File ET-2025-0184, Order Regarding Ameren Missouri's Request for Approval of a

 [8] MISO, Expedited Project Review Results and MISO Recommendation (Nov. 4, 2025), slides

 [9] Ameren Missouri, Ameren Missouri to Host Open Houses for Transmission Project in

Docket No. ER27-25-000                                                                                8
